es.summary: Disminución de la glucosa plasmática por debajo de los niveles normales, frecuentemente <70 mg/dL en diabéticos o <55 mg/dL en no diabéticos.
key_points: Glucosa <70 mg/dL en diabéticos indica hipoglucemia.
Síntomas neuroglicopénicos aparecen antes que los autonómicos.
Tratamiento inmediato: glucosa oral o dextrosa IV.
Beta‑bloqueadores pueden enmascarar los signos de alerta.
Prevención: comidas regulares, ajuste de fármacos y evitar alcohol.

pathophysiology: Exceso de insulina o secreción de insulina endógena reduce la glucosa plasmática.
Ayuno prolongado o ingesta insuficiente de carbohidratos disminuye la disponibilidad de glucosa.
Alcohol inhibe la gluconeogénesis hepática, favoreciendo la caída glucémica.
Medicamentos como sulfonilureas estimulan la liberación de insulina.
risk_factors: Ayuno prolongado o retraso en la comida.
Ejercicio intenso sin reposición de carbohidratos.
signs_symptoms: Confusión, irritabilidad, visión borrosa, somnolencia (síntomas neuroglicopénicos).
Pérdida de conciencia o convulsiones en casos graves.
diagnostics: Glucosa capilar <70 mg/dL (diabéticos) o <55 mg/dL (no diabéticos).
Evaluar electrolitos y función hepática si se sospecha causa secundaria.
treatment: Administrar 10‑20 g de glucosa oral (tabletas, jugo).
Si inconsciente, dextrosa al 50 % 25 mL IV bolus.
Glucagón 1 mg IM o SC si no hay acceso IV.
Reevaluar glucosa cada 15 min hasta >70 mg/dL.
Ajustar dosis de insulina o sulfonilureas según prescripción.
complications: Convulsiones y daño cerebral por neuroglicopenia.
Arritmias por hipocalemia secundaria al tratamiento.
nursing_care: Monitorear glucosa capilar cada 15‑30 min tras el episodio.
Evaluar nivel de conciencia y signos neurológicos.
Administrar glucosa según protocolo y registrar respuesta.
Mantener vía aérea permeable y posición lateral de seguridad si hay pérdida de conciencia.
Documentar causa probable y notificar al médico.
patient_teaching: Llevar siempre fuente rápida de glucosa (tabletas, jugo).
No omitir comidas y ajustar dosis de insulina antes de ejercicio.
Consultar al médico ante cambios en el patrón glucémico.

care_plans.diagnosis: Riesgo de nivel de glucemia inestable
outcomes: Glucemia estable: mantener entre 70‑180 mg/dL en 24 h.
Sin episodios de hipoglucemia durante la hospitalización.

interventions.action: Evaluar glucosa capilar cada 4 h y antes de cada comida.
interventions.rationale: Detectar rápidamente caídas glucémicas y prevenir complicaciones.

interventions.action: Educar al paciente sobre signos de hipoglucemia y uso de glucosa de acción rápida.
interventions.rationale: Facilita la autogestión y reduce tiempo de respuesta.

interventions.action: Revisar y ajustar dosis de insulina o sulfonilureas con el médico.
interventions.rationale: Previene exceso de insulina que causa hipoglucemia.

interventions.action: Asegurar disponibilidad de glucosa oral (tabletas, jugo) al alcance del paciente.
interventions.rationale: Permite tratamiento inmediato al primer signo.

interventions.action: Limitar consumo de alcohol y recomendar alimentos con carbohidratos complejos.
interventions.rationale: Reduce inhibición de la gluconeogénesis y estabiliza glucosa.

outcomes: Nivel de energía: reporta fatiga ≤3/10 en escala de 0‑10 en 48 h.
Participa en actividades de la vida diaria sin ayuda adicional.

interventions.action: Monitorear glucosa antes de actividades y proporcionar snack glucídico si <100 mg/dL.
interventions.rationale: Previene caída de energía durante la actividad.

interventions.action: Planificar descansos programados y fomentar sueño reparador.
interventions.rationale: Recupera reservas energéticas y mejora rendimiento.

interventions.action: Evaluar ingesta dietética y recomendar comidas balanceadas cada 3‑4 h.
interventions.rationale: Mantiene suministro constante de glucosa.

interventions.action: Registrar nivel de fatiga en escala de valoración cada turno.
interventions.rationale: Permite seguimiento de la respuesta a intervenciones.

interventions.action: Educar al paciente sobre la relación entre hipoglucemia y sensación de cansancio.
interventions.rationale: Fomenta autocuidado y reconocimiento temprano.

en.summary: Decrease in plasma glucose below normal levels, often <70 mg/dL in diabetics or <55 mg/dL in non‑diabetics.
key_points: Glucose <70 mg/dL in diabetics indicates hypoglycemia.
Neuroglycopenic symptoms appear before autonomic symptoms.
Immediate treatment: oral glucose or IV dextrose.
Prevention: regular meals, medication adjustment, avoid alcohol.

pathophysiology: Excess insulin or endogenous insulin secretion lowers plasma glucose.
Prolonged fasting or insufficient carbohydrate intake reduces glucose availability.
Alcohol inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis, favoring glucose drop.
Medications such as sulfonylureas stimulate insulin release.
signs_symptoms: Confusion, irritability, blurred vision, drowsiness (neuroglycopenic symptoms).
Loss of consciousness or seizures in severe cases.
diagnostics: Assess electrolytes and liver function if secondary cause suspected.
treatment: If unconscious, 50 % dextrose 25 mL IV bolus.
Glucagon 1 mg IM or SC if no IV access.
Reassess glucose every 15 min until >70 mg/dL.
Adjust insulin or sulfonylurea doses per prescription.
complications: Seizures and brain damage from neuroglycopenia.
Arrhythmias from hypokalemia secondary to treatment.
nursing_care: Monitor capillary glucose every 15‑30 min after episode.
Assess level of consciousness and neurological signs.
Administer glucose per protocol and record response.
Maintain airway and place in recovery position if unconscious.
Document probable cause and notify physician.
patient_teaching: Always carry a rapid source of glucose (tablets, juice).
Do not skip meals and adjust insulin before exercise.
Avoid alcohol on an empty stomach.
Consult physician if glucose pattern changes.

care_plans.diagnosis: Risk for unstable blood glucose level
outcomes: Stable glucose: maintain between 70‑180 mg/dL over 24 h.

interventions.action: Check capillary glucose every 4 h and before each meal.
interventions.rationale: Rapidly detect glucose drops and prevent complications.

interventions.action: Educate patient on hypoglycemia signs and use of rapid‑acting glucose.
interventions.rationale: Facilitates self‑management and reduces response time.

interventions.action: Review and adjust insulin or sulfonylurea doses with physician.
interventions.rationale: Prevents excess insulin causing hypoglycemia.

interventions.action: Ensure availability of oral glucose (tablets, juice) within reach.
interventions.rationale: Allows immediate treatment at first sign.

interventions.action: Limit alcohol intake and recommend complex carbohydrate foods.
interventions.rationale: Reduces gluconeogenesis inhibition and stabilizes glucose.

outcomes: Energy level: reports fatigue ≤3/10 on 0‑10 scale within 48 h.
Participates in daily activities without additional help.

interventions.action: Monitor glucose before activities and provide carbohydrate snack if <100 mg/dL.
interventions.rationale: Prevents energy drop during activity.

interventions.action: Plan scheduled rest breaks and promote restorative sleep.
interventions.rationale: Replenishes energy reserves and improves performance.

interventions.action: Assess dietary intake and recommend balanced meals every 3‑4 h.
interventions.rationale: Maintains constant glucose supply.

interventions.action: Record fatigue level on assessment scale each shift.
interventions.rationale: Tracks response to interventions.

interventions.action: Educate patient on link between hypoglycemia and fatigue.
interventions.rationale: Encourages self‑care and early recognition.

key_points.3.quote: Beta blockers can mask the early symptoms of hypoglycemia, such as tachycardia and tremors.

sections.pathophysiology.0.quote: Repaglinide is a meglitinide that works in clients with type 2 diabetes by closing potassium channels in the pancreatic beta cells, thereby increasing insulin secretion, which lowers glucose levels in the blood.

sections.pathophysiology.3.quote: Sulfonylureas are a group of diabetes drugs that bind to potassium channels on β cells and stimulate them to produce more insulin.

sections.risk_factors.0.quote: Sulfonylureas are a group of diabetes drugs that bind to potassium channels on β cells and stimulate them to produce more insulin.

sections.risk_factors.2.quote: If you drink too much alcohol without enough food.

sections.signs_symptoms.0.quote: Report symptoms of hypoglycemia such as headache, nervousness, sweating, clammy skin, tremor, and tachycardia.

sections.signs_symptoms.1.quote: Adverse effects of glipizide include headache, irritability, sweating, tachycardia, dizziness, nausea, blurred vision, feeling shaky, hypoglycemia, drowsiness, tremor, insomnia, myalgia, weight gain, and paresthesia.

sections.signs_symptoms.2.quote: Adverse effects include blurred vision, drowsiness, excessive hunger, headache, nausea, nervousness, sore throat, and unusual tiredness.

sections.signs_symptoms.3.quote: Because the brain needs glucose to function, severe hypoglycemia, or not enough glucose for a prolonged period, can impair the function of the infant’s brain, causing seizures and brain injury .

sections.patient_teaching.1.quote: Also carry a source of fast-acting carbohydrate, such as glucose tablets or a juice box, with you in case your blood glucose gets too low.
